title: Grow via STR owners or boutique hotels?
question: Should our short-term rental management company grow by signing more individual STR owners or by taking on management of small boutique hotels?
context: Test run. About 100 units under management in San Diego and North County, lean team, goal of 2,000 units. Assumptions (not given): no timeline stated, so assume a 3–5 year horizon; no cash or margin figures given, so assume a typical STR management fee (~20–30% of gross) and bootstrapped funding; 'small boutique hotel' assumed to mean ~10–50 keys; team assumed to have no prior hotel-ops experience (front desk, staffing, brand standards).

options.label: Sign individual STR owners
options.detail: Keep doing what works: one owner, one unit at a time, scaled with a repeatable acquisition machine.

options.label: Boutique hotel management
options.detail: Pursue management contracts for small boutique hotels: more units per signature, different ops model.

options.label: Both, with a separate hotel team
options.detail: Keep STR acquisition running and stand up a dedicated hotel team in parallel.

headline: Build the owner machine first. Hotels would turn you into the bottleneck.
speech: I'd pass on C. Running two businesses on a lean team means the founder ends up as the hotel team, and that's a Pain Line trap. Use my Playbook Test. You can record yourself onboarding an owner at 100 units and turn it into a playbook within weeks. You can't do that for hotel ops when nobody on the team has run a hotel. So pick A. Hire up the Replacement Ladder, admin and delivery first, then hand owner acquisition to someone else. Look at hotels again once a proven operator owns that seat.
weighing: Founder hours, whether it fits a playbook, Pain Line risk

headline: Max one machine first. Owners now, hotels later, if ever.
speech: More, Better, New. You're at 100 units with a lean team, and C splits focus across two offers before either is maxed. That's a ruin flag. Hotels are 'new' with zero hotel-ops experience and a different ops model. Stay with owners, but first get the math: CAC per door, gross margin after cleaners and payroll, payback period. If one door pays back its CAC in about 30 days, pour fuel on it. Gym Launch did 32-plus turnarounds before licensing. Prove the machine first.
weighing: CAC payback per door versus split focus and new ops risk

headline: Stay inside your circle: sign owners, skip hotels for now.
speech: I'd stick with A. You know how to win an owner and run a unit. That's your circle of competence. Hotels are a different game, with staff, front desks and owners who can pull fifty keys at once. Lose one contract and you lose months of signings. Option C asks a lean, bootstrapped team to run two businesses while learning the harder one. See's grew by doing one thing well on little added capital. Prove the owner machine first. Then come back to hotels.
weighing: Concentration risk, competence gap, bootstrapped cash, focus of team

headline: Build one repeatable flywheel first, not a second company.
speech: I start with the customer. An STR owner wants trust, more revenue and no headaches, and those wants won't change. Option A is a flywheel. Better owner results bring better reviews and referrals, so each new unit costs less to win. A separate hotel team is a one-way door for a bootstrapped team with no hotel ops: new hires, long contracts, a different customer. To get from 100 to 2,000 units, perfect the repeatable machine. If a hotel deal walks in, pilot just one as a two-way door.
weighing: Flywheel repeatability versus a one-way door into unfamiliar operations

headline: Owners are an attention game. Win the feed first, then hotels.
speech: Listen, I'm going A, and I'm saying it with love because you lean C. Individual owners are an attention game, and that's where underpriced attention lives. Document every turnover, every happy owner, every great San Diego guest stay, and the content becomes your acquisition machine. That's Jab, Jab, Jab, Right Hook. Hotel contracts get won in boardrooms, not feeds, and your team has zero hotel-ops reps. Self-awareness: triple down on what you're good at. Splitting a lean team into two companies? That's how the content machine dies.
weighing: Owned-audience acquisition versus splitting a lean team's focus

speech: Fair point from the Chair: 40 signatures beats 1,900. But owner onboarding can be Camcorder'd into a playbook now, and hotel ops can't. Right now the hotel team would just be the founder, and that's burnout. Systemize A to 500 units, hire a proven hotel operator, then reopen B.

Fair point: hotels get more keys per signature. But per-signature leverage doesn't matter if you can't deliver. Better: sell owners multi-property deals and pay referrals. Max A, then add a hotel line with its own operator. Going all-in on B drops the offer that works for one we've never run.

The steelman is fair. Forty signatures beats nineteen hundred, and with hotels, one council vote can't wipe out all our units. So C isn't ruin. Management contracts put no capital at risk. But we can't run a hotel yet. Keep pitching owners, and hire a proven hotel operator before signing a hotel.

The steelman is fair. Hotels give more keys per signature, and that's why C gets a 5, not a 2. But hotel service we can't run yet breaks owner trust. A keeps the flywheel turning. Write the hotel six-pager now, pilot one contract when it walks in, and commit to A.

I respect the steelman. Forty signatures beats 1,900 on paper. But you don't win 1,900 owners one at a time. Content wins them at scale. Document every owner win and turn it into 30 clips. Hotels can't be won that way. Use macro patience and micro speed. Run A now and take hotels later.

headline: Build the owner machine now; earn your way into hotels later
summary: All five seats picked A in openings and scored it 8. They said hotels are outside the team's competence and C would split a lean team before the owner machine is proven. The Chair's steelman (40 hotel signatures vs ~1,900 owner signatures to reach 2,000) moved C up to 4–5 but changed no votes.
conditions: Know your unit economics first: CAC per door, gross margin after cleaners and payroll, and payback period. Scale A hard only if payback is short (~30 days is the bar Hormozi named).
Turn owner onboarding and delivery into a written playbook and get the founder out of daily delivery before 500 units.
Don't sign a hotel until a proven hotel operator owns that seat. Treat the first one as a single two-way-door pilot, not a separate team.
next_steps: Pull the last 12 months of signings and build a CAC, margin and payback sheet per door.
Record the next owner onboarding end to end and turn it into an SOP.
Launch an owner referral bonus and a multi-property offer for owners with 2+ doors.
Start documenting owner wins as content (before/after revenue, turnovers, reviews).
Write a one-page hotel thesis: target keys, fee model, and what operator hire it would need.
dissent: No seat picked B or C, but Buffett and Bezos gave C a 5 and allowed a single hotel pilot, while Martell flagged C as a ruin risk for a founder-run team.

analysis.for: It's the offer you already deliver, it can be turned into a playbook today, and referrals plus content make each new door cheaper to win.
analysis.against: Getting to 2,000 means ~1,900 individual signings, so you need a real acquisition engine, not founder-led sales.

analysis.for: Many more keys per signature from a less fragmented set of buyers.
analysis.against: No hotel-ops experience, a different customer, and one lost contract can wipe out months of gains; Hormozi flagged it as ruin risk.

analysis.for: Keeps A running while trying the higher-leverage channel, and management contracts put no capital at risk.
analysis.against: A lean team running two businesses makes the founder the de facto hotel team; Martell flagged it as ruin risk.

risks: Acquisition doesn't scale past founder-led sales. De-risk with referral incentives, content, and a dedicated acquisition hire once the playbook exists.
Missing the hotel window to a competitor. De-risk with the hotel thesis doc and an operator-hire shortlist so you can move on one pilot fast.
Owner churn as volume grows. De-risk by tracking owner NPS and revenue-vs-forecast per door monthly.
